title_original: ‘My body started consuming itself. I was a millimetre from death’: Andrey Zvyagintsev on Covid, Putin and life in exile
excerpt_original: The Russian film-maker spent 40 days in a coma and suffered 92% lung damage during the pandemic. He describes how making new movie Minotaur helped his rehabilitation Andrey Zvyagintsev tells the tale of a knight who is riding through a dark forest and sees a stone sign at a fork…

blocks.text: A ndrey Zvyagintsev tells the tale of a knight who is riding through a dark forest and sees a stone sign at a fork in the road. The sign says that if he turns left he will lose his horse and if he turns right he will lose his head. So the knight has a dilemma; there are only bad options here. Zvyagintsev smiles and says: “It is a very Russian fairytale.”

Terrible things tend to happen, that’s the way the world works, and a person is defined by how they respond to each challenge. That goes for the knight in the forest and the characters in a film. It probably goes for Zvyagintsev, too, who has lost not his horse but his home and very nearly his life. The Russian director almost died during the Covid-19 pandemic and spent 40 days in an induced coma . He now lives in exile as an enemy of the state. “I’m with the birds,” he says by way of explaining his situation. “Birds have no borders. They’re not thinking about tomorrow.”

links.text: almost died during the Covid-19 pandemic and spent 40 days in an induced coma

blocks.text: Zvyagintsev’s new film, Minotaur, is a mighty, mesmerising drama of personal and political corruption that has Ukraine as its touchstone, or perhaps its dark fork in the road. He makes no bones about his opposition to the war. Taking the stage at this year’s Cannes film festival, where Minotaur won the grand jury prize, he called on Vladimir Putin to “stop this butchery”, adding that “the whole world is waiting”. In September Russia named him as a “foreign agent” spreading disinformation. He now risks arrest and imprisonment if he dares to go home.

blocks.alt: Iris Lebedeva, in a long beige coat, walks briskly along a park path, glancing back
blocks.caption: Mesmerising drama … actor Iris Lebedeva in Minotaur. Photograph: © MK Productions/CG Cinema

blocks.text: Today he is living out of a suitcase in a central London hotel; sipping bottled water and buffing the lenses of his specs. At 62, Zvyagintsev has the air of a college professor hosting a one-on-one tutorial. He’s erudite and charismatic, peppering his answers with quotes from Borges, Nietzsche and Savonarola. Who’s Savonarola? “A medieval friar,” he says. “A Catholic preacher. Very fierce.”

Zvyagintsev looks well but explains that his health is precarious. “My illness in 2021, 2022 has been following me ever since. It caused irreversible damage and presents serious challenges to the peripheral nervous system. So I’m not confident in my steps. I spend a lot of energy just to keep my balance. In Cannes, if you remember, I stumbled going up the steps to collect the award.” He shrugs. “Maybe you didn’t notice. My friends all noticed. Zoe Saldaña noticed. She had to reach out and catch me.”

There are no stumbles in Minotaur: it barely puts a foot wrong. Zvyagintsev’s film tells the tale of Gleb (Dmitriy Mazurov), a businessman caught between the proverbial rock and hard place. Gleb suspects that his wife may be having an affair, but he has also been asked to sacrifice 14 employees to fight on the frontline. Ukraine, one comes to realise, is the film’s peripheral horror and malign guiding spirit. The war is at once a faint, distant rumble and a monster so present that it might be breathing down Gleb’s neck.

blocks.alt: A man in a tan coat looks tensely at his own reflection in a bathroom mirror
blocks.caption: Dmitriy Mazurov as businessman Gleb in Minotaur. Photograph: © MK Productions/CG Cinema

blocks.text: Minotaur, Zvyagintsev’s first film since 2017’s acclaimed Loveless , is a loose remake of Claude Chabrol’s 1969 thriller La Femme Infidèle. The director explains that he initially tried to make it back in 2018 but wasn’t able to obtain the rights. “Looking back now, this was a good resolution. It would have been a completely different film, without any historical context.” Ukraine provided the project with the spark that it needed. Tangentially perhaps, his illness did too.

In the summer of 2021, he was given the Sputnik V Covid vaccine and came down with a fever. He was transferred from Moscow to a hospital in Germany where his condition became critical. Insofar as he knew what was happening, Zvyagintsev feared the worst. “August 2021. I associate it with death. Because the reality is that I should have died. Every day, that’s what my wife heard from the doctors. ‘Be ready, be prepared. It could be today.’ They were signing me off to the afterlife.”

Was the vaccine to blame? He shrugs. “No one knows. Symptom-less Covid – it seems that’s what it was. Then on top of that I had the vaccine, which set off a big storm. The bacteria entered my body and beat my immune system. My body started consuming itself. It’s a terrible thing. It is called Klebsiella [a bacteria that can cause pneumonia]. I had 92% lung damage and spent 40 days in an artificial coma. Full disconnection. A millimetre from death. And so afterwards you have to build everything from the ground.”

The director was in hospital for 11 months – first in Wiesbaden, then in Hanover. For much of that time he was at least partly paralysed by polyneuropathy and had to relearn how to use a knife and fork. He was on the ward when he heard Russia had invaded Ukraine. “My first thought was that it was no longer my country. That I must now live in a different country.”

Zvyagintsev seems to have broken with Russia in the way that Hemingway heroes go bankrupt: gradually, then suddenly. The government loved him when his 2003 debut, The Return , won the Golden Lion at Venice, and international critics were hailing him as the successor to Eisenstein and Tarkovsky. But it disliked 2011’s Elena, with its bleak portrait of life on Moscow’s dilapidated housing estates, and outright hated his 2014 masterpiece Leviathan , which painted the country as a hotbed of corruption and Christian nationalism. Leviathan, said Vladimir Medinsky, the then-minister of culture, was “opportunistic”, unrepresentative of “real Russians” and part of a new breed of films that “defiled” the motherland. Medinsky, incidentally, now serves as Moscow’s chief negotiator in peace talks regarding the war in Ukraine.

blocks.alt: person sits on a rock, looking out at a lake, next to a whale skeleton on the shore.
blocks.caption: Leviathan (2014) was criticised by the Russian government. Photograph: Anna Matveeva/Sony/Kobal/REX/Shutterstock

blocks.text: As for Zvyagintsev, he was simultaneously tracking Russia’s shift and drift under Putin. “There have been so many changes in these past 26 years,” he says. “They’re hard to trace. I’m not a specialist, I only know that around 2011, 2012, there was a crack in society. And in 2022 the crack became a collapse. The war is a catastrophe.”

The authorities claim he is a paid agent of the west. And in one sense they are right. Minotaur was shot in Latvia with French funding and has since been selected as France’s official submission for the Oscars. But it is a Russian film at heart, he says. “I know how the Russian press works. Not just the press. Instagram. Social media. Of course they will say that I’m working under orders, doing someone else’s will. I know the rhetoric. I get it. But this film isn’t [anti-Russian] propaganda. It’s a scream for help.”

Zvyagintsev now lives in Paris with his wife, Anna, and teenage son, Pyotr. He chose France over Germany because he regards it as a natural haven for film-makers; also Anna and Pyotr speak the language. But the adjustment has been hard and he doubts they’ll ever truly fit in. “So it’s a constant stress. Everything is new. The boy in particular has had a difficult time. In Russia he had friends. Here it is zero. Everything’s gone.” He smiles. “We’re like a family of astronauts in zero gravity.”

The knight in the forest has a hard choice to make. So does Gleb, the businessman in Minotaur, who has been tasked with delivering names to the draft board. Zvyagintsev says that no one in the world is intrinsically good or evil. Instead, they’re a complex series of arrows and vectors. Some turn left, some turn right and some remain in one place and leave it for others to decide.

blocks.alt: Film director Andrey Zvyagintsev poses seated in glasses and a grey blazer, hands clasped
blocks.caption: ‘My first thought was that it was no longer my country’ … Zvyagintsev. Photograph: Antonio Olmos/The Guardian

blocks.text: The director insists he has no regrets. He stands by his decision to make his films and speak out. “If you don’t do anything you become a pawn on the board. You can be pulled around, compromised. You’re a marionette on a string.”

Zvyagintsev knows he should have died and feels it’s a miracle that he didn’t. I tell him that his post-Covid existence amounts to an unlikely third act. It might not be the one he’d have chosen, I say, but it beats the alternative. The director nods. “Better than laying in the ground,” he agrees.

The director was so sick before he began shooting Minotaur, but the production was a breeze, it felt as if he was flying. This makes him think that film-making itself was his real rehabilitation and that he only needs to keep going in order to fully build up his strength. He plans to make another feature next year, possibly in English or French, and then another one after that, who knows?

Zvyagintsev peers at me through his specs, like a kindly professor gently correcting a student. He says, “I’m not sure that you’re right about this being a third act. That makes it sound like I’m finishing my life. I think it’s the third act of a four-act play. With an epilogue. And a sequel.”
